Issued at 321 AM EDT Fri Sep 25 2026

Today-Tonight... An upper level trough off the North 
Carolina/Virgina coast will slowly shift northward, becoming cut-off 
by tonight into Saturday. At the surface, the cold front across 
South Florida will continue to shift southward through the day, 
eventually pushing into the Straits of Florida by tonight. Locally, 
the pressure gradient will remain fairly tight, with northerly winds 
forecast to be 15-20 mph (10-15 mph well inland) with gusts 25-30 
mph (highest toward the coast). Drier air will continue to filter 
across the area today, with forecast PW values around 1.3-1.5" this 
afternoon, which will help limit convection. There is a low to 
medium (20-40 percent) chance of rain, mainly along the coast and 
around Lake Okeechobee. Main storm hazards today will be heavy 
downpours of 1-3", brief gusty winds of 40-50 mph, and occasional 
lightning strikes. 

Hazardous beach and marine conditions will persist today due to these 
strong north to northeast winds. Dangerous life-threatening rip 
currents, and rough surf will continue with large, breaking waves of 
4-8 ft. Expect minor coastal flooding along the Volusia coast and 
intracoastal waters. Residents and visitors should stay out of the 
dangerous surf.

Temperatures will be seasonable to slightly below normal for this 
time of year, with afternoon highs in the low to mid 80s. Due to the 
drier air, peak heat indices will be in the mid 80s to mid 90s. Lows 
are forecast to dip into the 60s for the first time since June (see 
Climate section below for dates).

Saturday-Monday... Upper level cut-off low pressure system off the 
North Carolina/Virgina coast Saturday will steadily lift northward, 
eventually pushing onshore across the New England coast by early 
next week. At the surface, weakening high pressure will shifts into 
the southeast US as high pressure across the western Atlantic will 
slowly build westward towards the Caribbean. At the same time, the 
frontal boundary that pushed through the Florida peninsula on 
Thursday, will stall across the Straits of Florida through the 
period. Locally, the pressure gradient will loosen as the cut-off 
low pushes northward and the high pressure moves into the SE US. 
North to northeast winds are forecast to increase to 10-15 mph with 
gusts to 25 mph Saturday afternoon, mainly along the coast, before 
decreasing to 5-10 mph and veering east to southeast through the 
rest of the period.  Drier air will filter across the local area, 
with forecast PW values ranging from 0.8-1.1" through Sunday before 
moisture begins to increase on Monday (PW values 1.3-1.5"). This 
will result in below normal rain chances Saturday and Sunday before 
becoming near normal for portions of east central Florida on Monday 
with a return of lightning storm chances as well. There is a low (20 
percent) chance of rain on Saturday across southern Treasure Coast, 
no mentionable rain chances (less than 10 percent) on Sunday, and a 
low to medium (20-30 percent) chance of rain across the Treasure 
Coast and around Lake Okeechobee on Monday.

Despite the winds decreasing, significant beach and marine hazards 
will continue through the weekend. A High Risk of rip currents, 
rough surf and a long period swell, which may cause minor beach and 
dune erosion, will continue at all area beaches through the weekend. 
A Small Craft Advisory will remain in effect for all the Atlantic 
waters through Saturday morning, with portions of the waters 
remaining in an SCA through at least the weekend. Entering the surf 
is not advised through at least the weekend. 

Seasonable to slightly below normal temperatures are forecast this 
weekend before becoming more seasonable early next week. Afternoon 
highs will be in the low to mid 80s Saturday and Sunday before 
increasing to mid to upper 80s on Monday. Morning lows will continue 
to be cooler, with temperatures in the 60s each day.  

Tuesday-Thursday... Upper level trough over the eastern seaboard 
early next week will push off shore by midweek. A surface high 
pressure in the western Atlantic will slowly shift northward through 
the period. Model solutions begin to diverge later into the period. 
The global models vary slightly in timing and location of a mid-
upper level trough and associated surface low swinging across the 
CONUS, bringing the attendant surface front towards Florida mid to 
late next week. Locally, onshore winds will remain in place, 
although there is some uncertainty if the winds will be more 
easterly or southeasterly. Moisture looks to recover slightly, 
however exactly how much remains in questions as forecast PW values 
range from near to below normal to above normal depending on the 
model. This has resulted in decreasing confidence in forecast rain
